lead: A program that talks to nobody is a calculator nobody can reach. Python gives two built-in functions for the conversation with the user: print() writes values to the screen, and input() reads one line typed at the keyboard, always as a string. Comments let you leave notes for humans that the interpreter skips. Indentation, the spaces at the start of a line, is how Python knows which lines form one block. These four habits decide whether a program is readable, whether it accepts marks as numbers, and whether it runs at all.
prereq: You need 1.6 for the expressions you put inside print() and around input(), and 1.5 for why a string and an integer behave differently.

sections.h3: Output: print() and its two edges

blocks.text: print() takes zero or more items and writes them to the screen, then moves to a new line. Each item is converted to text before it is shown, which is why a string and a number can sit in the same call: print("Total:", 10) works. By default print() puts exactly one space between items. Called with no items at all, print() prints just a newline.

blocks.where: item1, item2 … are the values to show, in order; sep is the text placed between items, default one space; end is the text placed after the last item, default \n, meaning go to the next line. Both sep and end must be strings.

blocks.text: Two keyword arguments change those edges. sep replaces the space between items, so a comma list comes out of sep=", ". end replaces the newline, so end="" keeps the cursor on the same line and the next print() continues there. A table row built by hand is just a careful choice of these two.

blocks.code:
a = 7
b = 3
print(a, b)
print(a, b, sep=", ")
print(a, b, sep="-", end=".\n")
print("Total:", a + b)

blocks.text: Note the last line: a+b is computed first, giving 10, and print() then shows a string and an integer side by side. print() itself returns nothing useful; you call it for what appears on the screen.

sections.h3: Input: input() always hands back a string

blocks.text: input() reads one line from the keyboard and returns it as a string. Type 87 and you get the two-character string "87", not the number 87. The text inside the brackets is the prompt: input("Enter marks: ") shows Enter marks: and waits on the same line, so the user knows what to type.

To get a number, convert the string. int(input("Marks: ")) works from the inside out: the prompt appears, the user types, a string comes back, and int() turns that string into a whole number. Use float() for decimals such as 72.5. int("87") succeeds; int("87 marks") raises ValueError because the text is not a plain number.

The prompt is a convenience only. On a phone or a web form the user may type into a box, but the rule stays: whatever arrives is text, and you convert it before doing arithmetic. Reading many lines in a loop is Unit 2 work; reading a whole file instead of one line is Unit 5.

sections.h3: Comments: notes the interpreter throws away

blocks.text: A comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line. Python discards it before running, so it costs nothing and exists only for the human reader. A full-line comment explains the block below it; a trailing comment explains one statement.

blocks.code:
charge = 0.05   # service charge, 5 percent
print("#1 in the class")   # the hash is inside a string here

blocks.text: A # inside a string is just a character, as the second line shows. A triple-quoted string (''' … ''' or """ … """) is not a comment: it is a real string value. When such a string stands alone as the first line of a file or a function, it is called a docstring and Python keeps it as documentation. Ordinary # comments are gone from the running program.

Python uses no braces to mark a block. The spaces at the start of a line decide which lines belong together. A header line that ends with a colon — an if header, a loop header, a def header — needs at least one indented line under it. All lines with the same indent belong to the same block, and the block ends when the indent drops back to an earlier column.

items: Four spaces per level is the usual convention; any consistent count works, but four is what most code uses.
Never mix tabs and spaces. The file can look perfectly aligned on your screen and still raise IndentationError or TabError.
Blank lines and lines holding only a comment are ignored when Python checks indentation, so they never break a block.

blocks.text: A long line can be split inside open brackets, or after a backslash: total = 1000 + 2000 + \ with 3000 on the next line is one statement. Open brackets are safer than the backslash, because a trailing space after a backslash is an error you cannot see.
Body statements that sit under if and while headers are Unit 2; here, fix the geometry — header, colon, indented body, same indent for equals.

figure.caption: The prompt is printed before any typing happens, and input() hands back the text as a string, which print() then shows in the greeting. Notice the value travels as a string from the keyboard to the screen unless you convert it.

spec.title: One prompt and one greeting
spec.aria: A chain from the input prompt, to the name variable holding Ravi, to print, to the greeting Hello Ravi on screen.

examples.question: Write a program that asks for a name and a birth year, then prints: Ravi, you are 24 years old in 2025. The user types Ravi and 2001. Show the value held by each variable at every step.
steps: name = input("Name: ") — the prompt Name: appears and input() waits. The user types Ravi, so name holds the string "Ravi".
year = int(input("Birth year: ")) — the prompt appears, the user types 2001, input() returns the string "2001", then int() converts it to the integer 2001 and year holds 2001.
The expression 2025 - year is evaluated: 2025 - 2001 = 24, an integer.
The first print item is name + ", you are", string concatenation giving "Ravi, you are".
print("Ravi, you are", 24, "years old in 2025") joins the three items with one space each, giving: Ravi, you are 24 years old in 2025.

The prompts stay on the screen as well. Each prompt is written without a newline, so the transcript reads Name: Birth year: Ravi, you are 24 years old in 2025. The typed characters do not show here because the input comes from a file; a person typing at the keyboard sees Ravi and 2001 sitting between the two prompts.
examples.answer: The greeting line is Ravi, you are 24 years old in 2025, and the age shown is 24 years. The prompts appear before it, so the full on-screen text is Name: Birth year: Ravi, you are 24 years old in 2025.

code.code:
name = input("Name: ")
year = int(input("Birth year: "))
print(name + ", you are", 2025 - year, "years old in 2025")

examples.output: Name: Birth year: Ravi, you are 24 years old in 2025

traps: Forgetting int() around input(). With the user typing 2001, the expression 2025 - input() raises TypeError, because the value is the string "2001"; the error message shows the value in quotes, which is your clue.
Using + where print() already separates. print("Total:", 5) is fine, but "Total:" + 5 raises TypeError; string + number needs str(5) first.

Double separators. A string that already ends in a comma and a space adds to the space print() supplies. print(name + ", ", "you are", 24) with name holding "Ravi" gives Ravi,  you are 24, with two spaces after the comma. Write name + "," with no trailing space and let print() supply the single space: Ravi, you are 24.
Mixing tabs and spaces, or adding one extra space before a line: the code looks aligned but Python raises IndentationError or TabError.
Calling # a comment when it sits inside quotes: print("#1") prints #1. Only an unquoted # starts a comment.

quiz.a: It always returns a string (str), even when the user types only digits.

quiz.q: Which character starts a single-line comment in Python?
quiz.a: The hash symbol #. It comments out everything from that point to the end of the line.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between sep and end in print().
quiz.a: sep is the text placed between two items, default one space. end is the text placed after the last item, default a newline, so the next print() starts on a fresh line.

quiz.q: The user types 45. What exactly is printed by: x = input(); print(x + "5")?
quiz.a: x holds the string "45". String + string concatenates, so the output is 455. Using int(x) + 5 would give 50 instead.

quiz.q: Give the exact output of: print("a", "b", sep="", end="!")
quiz.a: sep is empty so no space appears between a and b, and end is ! so no newline: ab!

quiz.q: A student writes total = input("Marks: ") + 10 and the program stops with TypeError. Why, and what is the smallest fix?
quiz.a: input() returns the typed text as a string, and Python will not add an integer to a string. Wrap the call: total = int(input("Marks: ")) + 10. For decimal marks use float() instead of int().

quiz.q: Why does Python need indentation while C uses braces, and why must tabs and spaces not be mixed?
quiz.a: In Python the indent itself marks the block, so the layout a human reads is the structure the interpreter runs; there is no separate brace to disagree with it. Tabs and spaces are different characters that can look equal in width, so a line indented with one tab may not match a line indented with four spaces, and Python raises TabError or IndentationError.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real programs rarely keep raw print() calls for messages; they use the logging module so the amount of detail can be switched on and off without editing code. Command-line tools read arguments rather than prompting, through sys.argv or the argparse module. Code formatters such as Black rewrite indentation to four spaces automatically, and linters flag mixed tabs before they reach a colleague. Search for "Python logging", "argparse tutorial" and "PEP 8 indentation" to go further; string formatting with f-strings is Unit 3, and reading whole files is Unit 5.
